events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: “Fill the Ranks”: The Civil War and the University of Michigan
events.summary: “Fill the Ranks”: The Civil War and the University of Michigan explores how campus and community debated the issues that tore the country apart, how students and alums joined the fight, and how the University’s public mission began to conflict with its elite aspirations. Based on collections at the Bentley Historical Library. Developed by the Judy and Stanley Frankel Detroit Observatory and featuring the work of its student docents, “Fill the Ranks” includes historic artifacts, digital animations, and interactive elements spanning two floors. On display September 25, 2026-July 2, 2027 at the Judy and Stanley Frankel Detroit Observatory, 1398 Ann Street, Ann Arbor, 48109. View the exhibit during the Observatory’s open hours: Thursdays 12-5 pm, Fridays 12-11 pm, Saturdays 12-5 pm. “Fill the Ranks”: The Civil War and the University of Michigan is supported in part by the Inclusive History Project. To learn more, please visit inclusivehistory.umich.edu. Additional support provided by the University of Michigan’s U.S. at 250 initiative.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.title: EIHS Lecture: The Tribute: The 1963 March on Washington and the Gendered Politics of Freedom
events.summary: The 1963 March on Washington has become the standard bearer in American public memory for non-violent, political demonstration. With Martin Luther King, Jr.’s “I Have a Dream Speech” as one of the most recognizable moments of the event, the depth and the nuance of the March on Washington and the movement that shaped has rarely surfaced among and academic and popular discourse. With attention to widening the frame in which to analyze the 1963 March on Washington, historian Marcia Chatelain offers a new reading of the March from the vantage point of the gender dynamics that undoubtedly shaped it. Marcia Chatelain is the Penn Presidential Compact Professor of Africana Studies at the University of Pennsylvania. A historian of African-American life and culture, Dr. Chatelain has taught at the University of Oklahoma and Georgetown University. She is the author of three books: South Side Girls: Growing up in the Great Migration, Franchise: The Golden Arches in Black America, and How Bright the Path Grows: The Untold Story of the Women Who Made the March on Washington. Dr. Chatelain has received awards for her writing and teaching, including the 2021 Pulitzer Prize in History. This event presented by the Eisenberg Institute for Historical Studies. It is made possible in part by a generous contribution from Kenneth and Frances Aftel Eisenberg.

events.title: The Anishnaabek of Company K: The Union Army’s Largest Indian Regiment
events.summary: Company K of the 1st Michigan Sharpshooters was made up of 139 Odawa, Ojibway, and Potwatomi soldiers. They fought in pivotal battles at the end of the American Civil War while their respective tribal communities were engaged in battles of their own with the United States. In this talk, Eric Hemenway will explore the complexity of Indian country during the time, the struggles of Michigan’s Anishnaabek and ask the question “why fight for the United States?” Eric Hemenway is an Anishnaabe/Odawa from Cross Village, Michigan. His work centers on bringing Anishnaabe/Odawa history to the public and advancing Anishnaabek rights. For 20 years Eric worked for the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians Archives. While at LTBB, Eric worked on exhibits, signage, curriculum, public programs, litigation and extensive work under the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act. Eric’s partners include the National Park Service, the State of Michigan, Harvard University, Yale University, and numerous local schools in Northern Michigan. Eric received his honorary doctorate from Oakland University and has received numerous awards for his work on integrating indigenous history into public spaces. He is currently the humanities manager for the School of Environment and Sustainability at the University of Michigan. In this role, Eric looks to include more humanities into the environmental justice movement through sharing the history of Michigan’s first people, the Anishnaabek. This lecture is in conjunction with the exhibition “Fill the Ranks”: the University of Michigan and the Civil War, on display at the Frankel Detroit Observatory September 24, 2026-July 2, 2027. This program is presented with support from the University of Michigan’s U.S. at 250 initiative and the Inclusive History Project.

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: Student AIM Seminar: The State of Local LLMs
events.summary: In the last few months, there has been rapid development in the world of local LLMs, which can run in PCs and laptops with enough RAM and a GPU. Though still far behind from frontier models, local LLMs can still write code, transcribe handwritten notes to LaTeX, and perform other agentic tasks without sending any data to a third party. In this talk we will explore the wide range of local LLMs that exist, what sets them apart from each other and areas where they are still lacking. events.title: Optimal Second-best Menu Design: Evidence from Residential Electricity Plans
events.summary: Utilities increasingly sell electricity using complex menus of time-constant and time-varying price schedules. We study how to design such a menu to maximize social welfare in a second-best environment where the marginal private and external costs of generating electricity vary over time, institutional constraints prevent mandating time-varying pricing, and consumer behavior is distorted by frictions. We develop a model of plan choice, consumption, and intertemporal substitution with time-varying marginal social costs, and estimate it using administrative data from a large utility. We provide evidence of substantial intertemporal substitution in response to time-varying price incentives, and selection across plans based on multidimensional heterogeneity. While the current menu's time-varying plans substantially shift consumption from high-price to low-price hours, we find that they reduce social welfare. This loss is mitigated by information frictions. We show how to redesign the menu to simultaneously improve outcomes for consumers, the utility, and the environment.
events.imageAlt: Optimal Second-best Menu Design: Evidence from Residential Electricity Plans

events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

events.title: MCDB Seminar Series> The impact of genetic cheating on mammalian reproduction and speciation
events.summary: Abstract: Genetic elements compete for transmission to the next generation through meiosis, when haploid gametes are created from a diploid parent. Although Mendel's Law of Segregation states that each genetic element has an equal chance to transmit to the gametes, it is becoming increasingly clear that this law is often violated by selfish elements. This non-Mendelian transmission of selfish elements in meiosis is called meiotic drive with significant impacts on chromosome evolution and fertility. I will present two unpublished stories on meiotic drive and its impact on speciation, both of which take advantage of rich natural variations and species divergence in mouse species. Bio: Dr. Takashi Akera graduated from the University of Tokyo with a Ph.D. in Biophysics and Biochemistry in 2014. He conducted postdoctoral research at the University of Pennsylvania in the laboratory of Dr. Michael Lampson from 2015 to 2019. He received both Holtzer Award for outstanding postdoctoral research in Cell and Developmental Biology and Kaushal Award for excellence in postdoctoral research in Genetics from the University of Pennsylvania in 2018. Dr. Akera joined the NHLBI in 2019 as an Earl Stadtman tenure-track Investigator and has made fundamental advances in the understanding of genetic cheating and its impact on mammalian reproduction and speciation. He has received the 2024 NHLBI Outstanding Mentor Award and the 2026 Vilcek Prize for Creative Promise in Biomedical Sciences.

events.title: CREES Noon Lecture. Rehabilitative Postsocialism, Racialised Capital, and Yearning for Crip Horizon
events.summary: Drawing on her new book, *Rehabilitative Postsocialism: Disability, Sex, and Race in Eastern Europe*, Kateřina Kolářová will argue that postsocialism is essential to understanding neoliberal cultural politics, economic structures, and state policies worldwide. She will show how disability, sexuality, and race—though often rendered invisible—have shaped the postsocialist consensus in the Czech Republic and more broadly. The talk will focus on how discourses of “inadaptability” have contributed to racialized abandonment. Kolářová will examine how particular understandings of disability helped establish an ideal of rehabilitated, white postsocialist citizenship. She will also consider the “neoliberalization of race” and the “racialization of neoliberalism” (Mahtani and Roberts) within the specific historical and political context of the Czech Republic and post socialist Eastern Europe. Specifically, Kolářová will explore how portrayals of Roma people as “inadaptable (non)citizens” have been used to determine who belongs in shared public spaces and whose exposure to violence is treated as morally defensible. The talk will conclude by examining forms of resistance that open up alternative possibilities, or “crip horizons.” Kateřina Kolářová is associate professor of sociology at Charles University in Prague. Kolářová’s other recent work takes the feminist queer crip perspective to explore the bio-social dimensions of metabolism, “crip guts,” the relationship between human and non-human lives, and how we coexist with microorganisms, toxic chemicals, and other "unclean" elements/entities. She is currently working on a monograph exploring HIV and human-viral coexistence (forthcoming in 2027). She is a passionate forager, fermentation enthusiast, and an avid chaos gardener. Her book *Rehabilitative Postsocialism: Disability, Sex, and Race in Eastern Europe* (University of Michigan Press, 2025) is available on "Open Access." It was the winner of the 2019 Tobin Siebers Prize for Disability Studies in the Humanities. Open Access link to book: https://www.fulcrum.org/concern/monographs/xd07gw749 If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at crees@umich.edu. events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.title: CJS Noon Lecture Series | When Self-Empowerment Goes South (or East, More Precisely): Gender, Neoliberalism, and Romance Fraud in Japan
events.summary: Please note: This lecture will be held in person in East Hall 4448 and virtually on Zoom. If you are attending in person, we recommend entering East Hall using the Church Street entrance and taking the elevator to the 4th floor. The webinar is free and open to the public, but registration is required. Once you've registered, joining information will be sent to your email. Register for the Zoom webinar at: https://myumi.ch/rwr6E. Building on scholarship on changing gender and intimacy norms under neoliberalism in Japan, this lecture explores how these transformations are reflected in the realm of romance fraud. Drawing on two contrasting sets of empirical material—interviews with romance fraud victims and publications and interviews with followers and supporters of the fraudster ‘Ririchan the Grantee Gal’—the lecture argues that these seemingly disparate groups are connected by a common underlying dynamic: women's struggle for autonomy and/or recognition within a gendered social hierarchy. It examines how aspirations for self-empowerment and liberation, often intensified by neoliberal ideals of personal responsibility and self-realization, can paradoxically lead individuals towards both victimization and offending. Dr. Yutaka Yoshida is a lecturer in criminology at Cardiff University. His research explores romance fraud victimization, digital vigilantism, and far-right movements in Japan, with a particular interest in narratives, identity, and technology-mediated social harms. His current work examines how romance fraud victims make sense of their experiences and reconstruct their lives in the aftermath of victimization, drawing on psychosocial approaches. events.title: Michael Malis
events.summary: THURS | Jan 14 Sets 7pm & 8:30pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE About the Artist Michael Malis is a composer, pianist, and music educator based in Detroit, MI. Noted for his “jaw-dropping display of improvisational power” (All About Jazz), Malis is a recipient of Greek America Foundation’s 40 under 40 award. He has taught at the University of Michigan and Interlochen Arts Academy, and is now a doctoral student at the University of Michigan. As a recording artist, he has released 13 albums. His music has been described as “downright transcendental” (Maggot Brain Magazine) and “uncommonly mature” (Detroit Free Press). He was noted as “among the most compelling Detroit jazz musicians of his generation” ( Jazz From Detroit , University of Michigan Press). His compositions have been performed across the United States, including at Harvard University, the University of Maryland, The Owl (Brooklyn), and Orchestral Hall (Detroit). As a pianist, Malis has shared the stage with a diverse array of musicians, including Marcus Belgrave, Jeff “Tain” Watts, Robert Hurst, Gerald Cleaver, Jaribu Shahid, John Lindberg, William Hooker, A. Spencer Barefield, Tyshawn Sorey, Brandee Younger, J.D. Allen, and Marion Hayden. He has performed at the Yokohama Jazz Promenade (Yokohama, Japan), the Kennedy Center, Birdland (NYC), and The Stone (NYC). He is the founder of Other Tones, a concert series providing performance opportunities for local and national composer-performers. To date, Other Tones has presented 22 artists from 7 cities to Detroit audiences. All proceeds from concerts go to presenting artists. The series centers artists from underrepresented groups, presenting a majority of queer, BIPOC, and women or femme-identifying artists. RESERVE TABLE

events.title: Alyssa Allgood + Kzoo Jazz Project
events.summary: Fri | Jan 22 Sets 7pm & 9pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE About the Artist Alyssa Allgood is a jazz vocalist, songwriter, bandleader and 3X DownBeat Magazine Critics Poll Rising Star based in Chicago praised for her “force, clarity and jazz integrity” (NYC Jazz Record). She was just named a finalist in the 2026 Sarah Vaughan International Jazz Vocal Competition. Drawing from both the vocal and instrumental jazz traditions, Allgood performs heartfelt originals and contemporary arrangements of standards with a voice that moves from tender to bold, and “improvisational prowess” (DownBeat) that puts her at the center of the band’s conversation. The inaugural winner of the Ella Fitzgerald Competition, Allgood has commanded stages across North America and beyond, including the Chicago and Hyde Park Jazz Festivals, Dizzy’s, Birdland, Mezzrow, Blues Alley, the Jazz Showcase, the Green Mill, Rudy’s Jazz Room and the Century Room in the US, the Shadbolt Centre for the Arts, Frankie’s and Yardbird Suite in Canada, and Jazz at Lincoln Center Shanghai. As a recording artist, Allgood has released four full-length albums and two EPs, including her 2026 release, Leap , which received a 3.5 star review from DownBeat Magazine. Driven by a desire to reflect the full spectrum of contemporary life, Allgood has built a body of original work that is both jazz-rooted and emotionally honest. Her album, From Here , features original music recorded with internationally renowned musicians Geoffrey Keezer, John Patitucci, Kendrick Scot and Greg Ward, with two songs selected as finalists in both the John Lennon Songwriting Contest and the International Songwriting Competition. Critics have consistently praised Allgood’s lyrical expression and instrumental-like improvisation. Allgood’s sophisticated artistry has earned her recognition from highly respected jazz institutions. A semifinalist in the Shure Montreux Jazz Voice Competition, where jazz legend Al Jarreau led the jury, she has also received the David Baker Memorial Scholarship through the Jazz Education Network, a Jazz Improvisation Fellowship from the Luminarts Cultural Foundation, and recognition as 2X Chicago Reader Poll Best Individual Jazz Musician, a testament to her deep roots and devoted following in her hometown. Dedicated to mentorship, Allgood teaches jazz voice at Loyola University and offers private voice lessons online, empowering students to develop authentic expression and musical freedom. She holds a Master of Music in Jazz Studies from DePaul University and is a highly sought-after clinician, ensemble director and adjudicator and Grammy U mentor. Her teaching work has taken her to the Jazz Education Network Conference, the University of North Texas’s Jazz Lecture Series, the Illinois Music Educators Association, the Iowa Choral Directors Association, Anchor Music’s Vocal Jazz Academy, jazzvoice.com and the University of Chicago. Her next album is scheduled to release in Spring 2027. Co-produced by 2X GRAMMY-winning artist Nicole Zuraitis and developed through the Chamber Music America Performance Plus Grant, it represents Allgood’s most powerful work to date. Featuring her working Chicago quintet of Greg Ward on alto saxophone, Julius Tucker on piano, Ethan Philion on bass and Jon Deitemyer on drums, the album solidifies Allgood’s place as a vital force in the modern vocal jazz movement. events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.title: Algebraic Geometry Seminar: Valuatively independent bases for Calabi-Yau varieties
events.summary: From the perspective of the Gross-Siebert program, the mirror symmetry of Calabi-Yau varieties is governed by certain canonical bases for the sections of the powers of an ample line bundle on a degeneration. It is expected that the pairing between these basis elements and valuations in the essential skeleton satisfies an independence condition, similar to the pairing between monomials and monomial valuations on a toric variety. In this talk, I will explain how tools from birational geometry and K-stability can be used to construct bases that fulfill this condition. This is joint work with Yuchen Liu.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: The Franchise Gap: Fissuring, Job Quality, and Labor Standards Compliance
events.summary: Work has increasingly re-organized and fissured: the breakdown of traditional employment relations has pushed lower-income workers into lower-income firms (Weil, 2014), including through sub-contracting, outsourcing, and franchising. A growing empirical literature links such arrangements to declines in job quality along several dimensions, with studies of domestic outsourcing documenting sizable wage penalties (Dube and Kaplan 2010; Goldschmidt and Schmieder 2017) and generally elevated employment instability (Aeppli 2025). We contribute to the literature on fissuring and job quality by examining the case of franchising, which has gone relatively little examined due to limits of existing data. We take on this question by deploying two sources of novel linked data in the US context. First, we use a national individual-level sample of thousands of hourly workers employed at dozens of fast food firms surveyed between 2019 and 2025 collected by The Shift Project. These data provide both unusually detailed direct worker reports of job quality and the capacity to link responses at the firm level to organizational attributes. We make use of this capacity for linkage by leveraging a second source of novel data, legally required annual Franchise Disclosure Documents (FDDs), which report, by state and year, the number of company-owned and franchised outlets as well as detailed contractual provisions that aim to standardize production. We scraped state-firm-year level counts of franchised and company-owned establishments for major fast-food chains for the years 2019 to 2024. We show that workers in franchised fast-food restaurants make, on average, $1.7\hr less than workers in non-franchised fast-food restaurants, and have, on average, a 40-50 p.p. lower rate of access to paid sick leave and a stable schedule. In an overall job quality index, including dimensions such as wages, quality of hours worked, scheduling, fringe benefits, and work-life balance, franchisee companies have, on average, a score that is 3/4 of a standard deviation lower than that of non-franchise companies. Using the staggered implementation of Paid Sick Leave policies across 11 states, we show that these policies reduced the gap in access to PSL by 26 percentage points. Despite the substantial effect of the law’s introduction in reducing the gap, we also document rampant non-compliance with these laws: over 60% of workers in PSL jurisdictions in franchised establishments have their right to paid sick leave violated.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. events.title: Awakening the Dragon–Showcasing the Building and Performance of an Asian Icon
events.summary: Experience a curated experience of the imaginary, featuring a lightly sci-fi, magnificent work of art--the LRCCS Fortune and Longevity Dragon, a 25-ft long, Asian-inspired full-body dragon sculpture for use in the traditional "dragon dance" crafted by renowned international artist Zhen Guo with U-M faculty arts lecturer Raymond Wetzel, artist Jeri Rosenberg, students, and volunteers The exhibition highlights the story of the dragon's fabrication and its impact on community.. An iconic symbol of inclusivity, strength, and courage, this newly imagined U-M dragon, with its futuristic flair, technological creativity and sustainable materials, invites students and the entire community to re-envision a classic cultural symbol for contemporary times. events.title: The Terry Farmer Band
events.summary: Ticket prices on our website reflect all-in pricing for purchases made online or by phone. This means the price you see includes the ticket price plus MUTO’s ticket processing fee. Tickets may be purchased with no included fees in person at The Ark during box office hours. Terry is a seasoned professional musician. Starting from a young age in his family band, Terry’s music career has taken him to all four corners of the country and beyond as a player and band leader, including a 2-year stint as lead guitarist with surf legends Jan & Dean, and 3 years of national touring with his original rock & roll band, The Bead Band. In the 1990’s, after several years living in Los Angeles, he spent 6 years studying classical guitar at the University of Denver and the Cleveland Institute of Music. At the turn of the century Terry returned to his roots creating several solo CDs featuring a fusion of styles and players – and all original songs. events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: CMENAS 2026 Fall Colloquium Series | Western Sahara: Multi-scalar Struggles, Recognition and Change in a Thawing Conflict
events.summary: Irene Fernández-Molina is a senior lecturer in International Relations at the University of Exeter. She is a scholar of international relations of the Global South and across the Euro-Mediterranean space, contested statehood and international recognition politics, and foreign policy and conflicts in the Maghreb. She previously worked as a research fellow at the European Neighbourhood Policy Chair of the College of Europe (Warsaw), Schuman fellow at the Directorate-General for External Policies of the European Parliament (Brussels), and PhD research fellow at Complutense University of Madrid. Her research has been published in journals such as *International Affairs*, *International Studies Review*, *Review of International Studies*, *International Political Sociology*, and the *Journal of Intervention and Statebuilding*. She is the author of *Moroccan Foreign Policy under Mohammed VI, 1999–2014 *(2016), and co-editor of *Global, Regional and Local Dimensions of Western Sahara’s Protracted Decolonization* (2017), and* Foreign Policy in North Africa: Navigating Global, Regional and Domestic Transformations* (2021). events.title: Mozart & Schumann’s Romantic Rhenish
events.summary: Two DSO musicians step into the spotlight in a program of grace, elegance, and joy. Fanny Mendelssohn’s Overture—her only purely orchestral work—is paired with Robert Schumann’s “Rhenish” symphony, music alive with optimism, fire and a deep sacred glow. Flutist Hannah Hammel Maser and harpist Alyssa Katahara are soloists in Mozart’s Concerto for Flute and Harp. Join us for a pre-concert talk 1 hour before most performances (read more below). Enjoy this concert online at any of the following locations on Saturday, November 14 at 8:00pm ET: Live from Orchestra Hall: livefromorchestrahall.vhx.tv/live-broadcasts YouTube Live: youtube.com/@detroitsymphony/streams Facebook Live: facebook.com/detroitsymphony Pre-concert Talk Join us one hour prior to most classical performances for a 30-minute pre-concert talk. Pre-concert talks are an opportunity for conductors, musicians, and other experts to share more about the music and enhance your connection to the evening's program. You will get a glimpse into the composer's inspiration, the story behind a work, what to look for in a soloist's performance, and more! With a deeper understanding of the music, your symphony experience will be more engaging and even more memorable. Please note, our pre-concert talks are scheduled for every PVS Classical Series performance, except Friday morning Coffee Concerts. Insider tip: Seating for pre-concert talks is general admission in Orchestra Hall. Try out a different seat or section from your ticket for a new perspective.

events.title: Craft Lecture by Lars Horn
events.summary: Zell Visiting Writers Series craft lecutures are free and open to the public and will be offered both virtually (via Zoom) and in person (Michigan League, Henderson Room 3rd floor). Seats are offered on a first come, first served basis; please arrive early to secure a spot. Login here (no pre-registration needed): https://myumi.ch/ZellWriters26 Lars Horn is a writer and translator working in literary and experimental non-fiction. Horn’s first book, *VOICE OF THE FISH: A LYRIC ESSAY*, won the 2020 Graywolf Nonfiction Prize, the 2023 Great Lakes Colleges Association New Writers Award, and was named an Honor Book for the 2023 Stonewall Israel Fishman Nonfiction Book Award as well as an American Booksellers Association Indies Introduce Selection. Footnote Press acquired *VOICE OF THE FISH* for UK release in September 2022. In 2016, Horn translated the volume Ateliers & Studios for the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts. The recipient of the Tin House Without Borders Residency and fellowships from the Sewanee Writers’ Conference, the Kenyon Writers Workshops, and the Virginia Center for the Creative Arts, Horn’s writing has appeared in *Granta, the Virginia Quarterly Review, the Kenyon Review, Poets & Writers, The Rumpus, Literary Hub*, and elsewhere. Initially specialising in Phenomenology and Visual Arts scholarship, he holds MAs from the University of Edinburgh, the École normale supérieure, Paris, and Concordia University, Montreal as well as an MFA from Randolph College. He lives in New York and teaches at Columbia University. ASL interpreters and CART services at in-person events are available upon request; please email zvwseries@umich.edu at least two weeks prior to the event, whenever possible, to allow time to arrange services. events.summary: Experience a curated experience of the imaginary, featuring a lightly sci-fi, magnificent work of art--the LRCCS Fortune and Longevity Dragon, a 25-ft long, Asian-inspired full-body dragon sculpture for use in the traditional "dragon dance" crafted by renowned international artist Zhen Guo with U-M faculty arts lecturer Raymond Wetzel, artist Jeri Rosenberg, students, and volunteers The exhibition highlights the story of the dragon's fabrication and its impact on community.. events.title: The Rise and Fall of the NCAA: How We Got Into This Mess
events.summary: When the topic of revenue sharing with student-athletes came up in 2023, U-M Coach Jim Harbaugh loudly supported it, arguing that “The current status quo is unacceptable and won’t survive.” Those words proved prophetic and today the world of college athletics is in rapid flux. Join us to hear from Lecturer Greg Dooley to hear about how similar concerns led to the creation of the National Collegiate Athletic Association in 1906, how the organization evolved and grew in power, how that power has collapsed over the last decade, and what it means for the Wolverines. Greg Dooley is a devoted Michigan sports fan, having covered the history and culture of Michigan sports for over twenty years at his website MVictors.com. A full-time lecturer in the Marsal Family School of Education, he teaches courses on “The History of College Athletics” leadership through coaching, and on Name, Image, and Likeness (NIL) contracts. He also frequently appears as a guest on local radio shows, history documentaries, and as a speaker for university teams and alumni groups. Refreshments will be provided, and anyone is welcome to attend this free talk. Registration is recommended for in-person attendance, and we’re glad to welcome anyone who wishes to attend virtually. The Making Michigan series is co-sponsored by the Alumni Association of the University of Michigan.

events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: Comics Beyond Sight
events.summary: This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening. View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

events.summary: We are sorry to announce that our upcoming CSEAS lecture feature Lê Vân scheduled for 11/20 at 12 pm has been canceled due to unforeseen circumstances. We hope to offer this event again in another semester and will follow up once a new date is confirmed. Thank you for your understanding. ----- What happens to a war after the war is over? Vietnamese journalist and documentary filmmaker Van Le reflects on the Vietnam War through the memories of those who lived through it. Drawing on her years of reporting and documentary filmmaking, she explores how the war continues to shape Vietnamese identity, relationships, and understandings of the past—both in Vietnam and across the diaspora. The talk focuses on personal memories of loss, fear, displacement, loyalty, and silence, and how trauma is remembered, carried, and passed across generations. Van Le is an investigative journalist, author, and independent documentary filmmaker based in Vietnam. She is a 2026–2027 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She was a reporter for the acclaimed documentary The Stringer and has contributed environmental reporting to ProPublica. She previously worked as a feature writer and investigative journalist for Thanh Nien Newspaper, a national news outlet in Vietnam. *If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us. events.title: Christian Sands Trio
events.summary: Sat | Dec 5 Sets 7pm & 9pm $95 Dinner & Show $50 Cover Only RESERVE TABLE About the Artist Christian Sands – Steinway Artist and five-time Grammy Nominee – is an emerging jazz force. His abundant piano technique perfectly matches his conception, accomplishing a much deeper musical goal: a fresh look at the entire language of jazz. Whether it’s stride, swing, bebop, progressive, fusion, Brazilian or Afro-Cuban, Sands develops the past while providing unusual and stimulating vehicles for the present… and for the future. He expresses himself through an extensive vocabulary of patterns, textures and structures, all the while maintaining a strong sense of understatement, sensitivity, taste and swing. Jazz history is filled with stirring torch songs and ballads – brilliant expressions of suffering after love has gone awry. The jazz record shelf even contains some classic album-long explorations of melancholy. But it’s hard to find precedent in pianist Christian Sands’ new Embracing Dawn, his fifth full-length effort for Mack Avenue Records. Embracing Dawn trails 2023’s acclaimed Christmas Stories and 2020’s GRAMMY-nominated Be Water. Following that album’s release, the New York Times commented, “Equipped with a crisp but forceful touch, he seems always to be flowing in new directions, integrating elements of prog rock, gospel and Western classical into a forward-tumbling jazz conception.” Embracing Dawn furthers Sands’ uniquely cultivated jazz language, where agile post-bop meets soulful bluesy tinges and gorgeous swells of strings. Sands’ love of classical orchestration, he explains, is rooted in his lifelong obsession with film. Since arriving on the scene, Sands has shared the stage with such jazz luminaries as Wynton Marsalis, Dianne Reeves, Shelia E, Warren Wolf, Tia Fuller, Gary Burton, Stefan Harris, Terri Lyne Carrington, Jason Moran, Geri Allen, Ben Williams, Randy Brecker, Steve Johns, Avery Sharpe, James Moody, Bill Evans (sax), Russell Malone, Terence Blanchard, Louis Hayes, Patti Austin, Marcus Baylor, Craig Handy, Carl Allen, Kirk Whalum, and Wycliffe Gordon, as well as iconic cellist Yo-Yo Ma. The power and prowess of his playing has taken him from the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., to the world renowned Newport Jazz Festival, Detroit Jazz Festival, to New York’s celebrated jazz clubs such as the Village Vanguard, Jazz Standard, Blue Note and Dizzy’s Club; to international jazz clubs all over the world. Sands was Artist in Residence at the Monterey Jazz Festival from 2020-2022, Creative Director of Octave Music – Erroll Garner Estate from 2017-2021, and Musical Director of the Monterey Festival Band On Tour from 2019-2022. Sands invents and re-invents himself with sonorities which define each moment, rhythms which impel his music forward, structures which are surprising and fascinating – and never for a moment un-musical. He personifies the rising musicality and spiritual aspirations of a singularly gifted musical soul. “To whom much is given, much is expected.” Christian Sands doesn’t disappoint. RESERVE TABLE

events.title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
events.summary: Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering. As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting? On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

events.title: What Makes a Good Cop? Measuring Officer Quality and the Trade-Off Between Policing and Public Safety
events.summary: This paper measures heterogeneity in officers’ effects on reported crime and policing activities (stops, arrests, force use, and misconduct complaints) using Chicago administrative data. I estimate officer fixed effects for each outcome and compute their bias-corrected variances and covariances. Officers differ significantly in their effects on activities and crimes, with effects on serious crimes driving differences in effects on social costs. However, officers’ activity effects and crime effects are only weakly correlated, and activity effects and demographics explain little variation in crime and total-cost effects, suggesting that common measures of officer productivity poorly predict officers’ effectiveness at reducing crime.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

events.title: Tiffany Ng, carillon
events.summary: University Carillonist Tiffany Ng performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds. Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

A graduate of Stanford University's Symbolic Systems program, he took creative writing classes with Adam Johnson, ZZ Packer, and Elizabeth Tallent. After graduating, he published a handful of stories, one of which won an O. Henry Award, as he worked for a small Bay Area UX firm. He got accepted to the Iowa Writers' Workshop the same week he was laid off in 2010. At Iowa he finished most of a draft of his debut novel *Private Citizens*, which was called "the first great Millennial novel" by *New York Magazine* after its publication in 2016, and received a Whiting Writers' Award. In 2017 he founded CRIT, an independent class he teaches out of his apartment in Brooklyn, whose alumni have gone on to publish 34 books to date. He has written for *The Paris Review, N+1, The New York Times, The New Republic, The Believer, Playboy, The Nation,* and others. Tony's second book is a novel-in-stories, *Rejection*, published in 2024. *Rejection* has been translated into seven languages, and was nominated for the National Book Award, the Story Prize, and the Clark Prize, and received a Jack Galef Literary Arts award. He is currently a Visiting Professor at the Iowa Writers' Workshop. For any questions about the event or to share accommodation needs, please email zvwseries@umich.edu--we are eager to help ensure this event is inclusive to you. events.title: Steven Page
events.summary: Ticket prices on our website reflect all-in pricing for purchases made online or by phone. This means the price you see includes the ticket price plus MUTO’s ticket processing fee. Tickets may be purchased with no included fees in person at The Ark during box office hours. Over the last thirty-five years, Canadian Music Hall of Fame inductee Steven Page has established himself as one of the most recognizable and enduring voices in music. The release of his latest album, Excelsior, shows that he has no plans of slowing down anytime soon. As a co-founder, vocalist and songwriter for Barenaked Ladies, Steven sang and wrote classics like “Brian Wilson,” “If I Had A Million Dollars,” “What A Good Boy,” “It’s All Been Done” and many more. With the band, he sold over 15 Million albums and scored multiple Junos, Billboard Music Awards, SOCAN awards, Gemini Awards and two Grammy nominations. After leaving the band in 2009, Steven embarked on a solo career that has produced five solo albums, including 2022’s Excelsior, and has seen him tour worldwide, from folk festivals to cabarets and theatres, all the way to packed arenas on a string of dates opening for rock legends The Who. Steven performs in many configurations, but, since 2016, has been playing most often with his pals in The Steven Page Trio, Craig Northey of Vancouver legends Odds on guitar, and Kevin Fox on cello. With SP3, Steven has performed arrangements of some of his best-loved songs from his long career with symphony orchestras including the Vancouver and Winnipeg Symphony Orchestras. Steven is a frequent collaborator with Toronto’s eclectic Art of Time Ensemble, is a member of power-pop quartet, The Trans-Canada Highwaymen, has a Stratford commissioned musical in the works, and continues to work in film, television and other media. The Governor-General’s Performing Arts Awards asked Steven to write a song as a surprise tribute to his friend, Ryan Reynolds, and the result was “Canada Loves You Back,” a song as poignant, humorous and Canadian as the actor it honors.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Guest Lecture | Heritage Forensics: Culture on the Front Lines of the Armenia-Azerbaijan Conflict
events.summary: This talk introduces the concept of heritage forensics, a framework for studying abuses of cultural heritage in contexts of conflict, genocide, and ethnic cleansing. Drawing on the new co-authored volume, *Heritage Forensics: Cultural on the Front Lines of the Armenia-Azerbaijan Conflict*, the presentation examines how cultural sites became entangled in the conflict over Nagorno-Karabakh during the interwar period (1994-2020). The talk considers how satellite-based heritage forensics is being deployed prospectively, to monitor hundreds of Armenian sites in Karabakh following Azerbaijan's 2023 takeover of the region and the displacement of its Armenian population. In doing so, it asks: how can satellite-based monitoring function as a form of "counter-forensics," turning surveillance technologies developed for military purposes back on the state? Can heritage forensics move us beyond retrospective documentation to actively deter erasure and support truth, reconciliation, and accountability wherever cultural heritage is at stake? Lori Khatchadourian is Professor of Near Eastern Studies and Anthropology at Cornell University, and co-founder and co-director of Caucasus Heritage Watch. She currently serves as Director of the Cornell Institute of Archaeology and Material Studies. Khatchadourian’s research spans the fields of archaeology, social anthropology, and heritage studies, with a particular focus on Armenia, the wider South Caucasus, and neighboring regions. Current projects explore the archaeology of modernity, including problems of genocide, deindustrialization, and the entanglements of cultural heritage and war. She is the co-author of *Heritage Forensics: Culture on the Front Lines of the Armenia-Azerbaijan Conflict* (Cornell, 2026) and author of Imperial Matter: Ancient Persia and the Archaeology of Empires (UC Press, 2016). She is also co-editor of *Rethinking Empire: Materiality, Metaphysics, and Imperial Politics* (SAR, 2026) and *Fitful Histories and Unruly Publics: The Archaeology of Eurasia *(2017). https://umich.zoom.us/j/99311308952 Cosponsors: Center for Middle Eastern and North African Studies, Department of Middle East Studies, Department of Anthropology, Classical Studies, Center for Russian, East European, and Eurasian Studies, Ancient Mediterranean Art and Archaeology (IPAMAA) Kelsey Museum, Archaeology at Michigan, and NAASR. events.title: Dwight Adams
events.summary: Fri | Jan 29 Sets at 7pm and 9pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE About the Artist One blast from his trumpet, and it’s clear as day – Dwight Adams is the real deal. For more than two decades he’s been playing stages worldwide with Motown legend Stevie Wonder, but for even longer than that he’s been igniting audiences in the more intimate settings of Detroit’s greatest clubs. Dwight is a soul-inspired jazz trumpeter and one of the brightest stars on the Detroit jazz scene. And although he was, by his own account, a late-comer to his instrument – he didn’t pick up the trumpet until he was a junior in high school – hard work, natural talent and an unshakable dedication to being the best musician he could be helped him land his first gig at the age of 16, playing in Teddy Harris’ New Breed BeBop Society Orchestra. In addition to his countless tours with Stevie Wonder, Dwight has also played and recorded with world-renowned jazz artists including Marcus Belgrave, Rodney Whitaker, James Carter, Shawn Wallace and Donald Walden. He’s also been a member of the Columbus Jazz Orchestra, under the direction of Byron Stripling, since 2003. In 2015, he joined the Detroit Bop Quintet for a special reenactment session at Detroit’s legendary United Sound Studio. The group came together to recreate the acoustic footprint of four historic tracks. The tunes were recorded at the studio nearly seventy years earlier by Charlie Parker and his quintet for the Savoy label. The resulting tracks by the Detroit Bop Quintet prove if there’s anyone in Detroit that can invoke the spirit of Miles, it’s Dwight Adams. In addition to being a highly accomplished musician, Dwight is also a respected educator. He has taught in the jazz studies programs at Michigan State University and Ohio State University, and is currently part of the Wayne State University faculty. RESERVE TABLE

events.title: Mozart's Requiem and Brahms's Alto Rhapsody with Ann Arbor Symphony and UMS Choral Union
events.summary: While Mozart is not primarily known for sacred music, his final composition — the Requiem Mass — stands among his most sublime achievements. Left unfinished at his death at age 35 and immortalized in the film Amadeus, the work was commissioned anonymously by a mysterious benefactor and was ultimately completed by Mozart’s student, Franz Xaver Süssmayr, from his sketches. As Mozart’s health declined, he is said to have believed he was composing the Requiem not for another, but for himself, a notion that deepens the work’s haunting resonance. Blending fear and hope with extraordinary emotional depth, the Requiem has captivated listeners for centuries. This performance marks the UMS Choral Union’s first return to the piece in 80 years, in collaboration with the Ann Arbor Symphony Orchestra and its music director, Earl Lee. The program opens with Johannes Brahms’s rarely-performed Alto Rhapsody, a striking work for alto, male chorus, and orchestra. PROGRAM Johannes Brahms Alto Rhapsody, Op. 53 Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart Requiem in d minor, K. 626 Featuring: Ann Arbor Symphony Orchestra UMS Choral Union ( Scott Hanoian, UMS Choral Union music director) Earl Lee, music director and conductor Hera Hyesang Park, soprano Avery Amereau, mezzo-soprano Nicholas Phan, tenor Stephano Park, bass

events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: SRC Research Seminar Series: RESET Demonstration Project: Early Results and Long-term Aims
events.summary: Join Zoom Meeting https://umich.zoom.us/j/96393804480?pwd=ajnQfFv3GaVabRiIGyHpos27HLirqQ.1&jst=2 Meeting ID: 963 9380 4480 Passcode: 74720 Abstract: This seminar will present early results and the long-term aims of the RESET Demonstration Project, an initiative that constructs price and sales indices using item-level transaction data. The project’s overarching goal is to demonstrate the feasibility and advantages of leveraging modern transaction data for economic measurement, pointing toward a future in which official economic statistics are rebuilt using 21st-century data and technology. The seminar will present new measures of food-at-home inflation and evaluate them on two fronts: how they compare to current official statistics and what they offer as novel measures that more accurately capture the dynamics of consumer choice. It will also address the challenges of producing reliable and credible official statistics from item-level transaction data. The RESET Project is supported by grants from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation (G-2016-7227, G-2021-16821, G-2025-25236, G-2025-25273) and the National Science Foundation (2537470). The methodology and early results presented in this seminar are reported in “Early results from the RESET demonstration project: Inflation in food at home” Journal of Monetary Economics (In Press): https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmoneco.2026.103991 Bio: Matthew Shapiro is the Lawrence R. Klein Collegiate Professor of Economics and a Research Professor in the Survey Research Center at the University of Michigan. His general area of expertise is macroeconomics. His current work focuses on reengineering official economic statistics through his leadership of the Re-Engineering Statistics Using Economic Transactions (RESET) Project and the Economic Measurement Research Institute (EMRI) at the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER). Shapiro has a career-long interest in official statistics. He has served as chair of the Federal Economic Statistics Advisory Committee (FESAC)—the official advisory committee for the Census Bureau, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and the Bureau of Economic Analysis—as well as chair of the American Economic Association’s Committee on Economic Statistics (AEAStat) and a member of the National Academy of Sciences’ Committee on National Statistics (CNSTAT). Shapiro currently chairs the Academic Advisory Council of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago. Before joining the faculty at the University of Michigan, Shapiro was a faculty member at Yale University. He has twice served on the staff of the President’s Council of Economic Advisers. He was coeditor of the American Economic Review and editor of the American Economic Journal: Economic Policy. His administrative appointments at the University of Michigan have included chair of the Department of Economics and director of the Survey Research Center.

events.title: RTG SEMINAR GeometryTopologyDynamics:  TWO INVARIANTS OF TYPE-PRESERVING REPRESENTATIONS AND APPLICATIONS
events.summary: Abstract: We investigate the representations of surface groups into PSL(2, R). For a closed surface, by the classical result of Goldman, the Euler class provides a complete classification of the connected components of the character variety. However, describing these components becomes more subtle when considering the type-preserving representations for punctured surfaces. In this talk, I will introduce two invariants of type-preserving representations that characterize the connected components. As an application, I will show the existence of totally hyperbolic representations, giving a negative answer to a question of Bowditch. I will also discuss the relation between the existence of such representations and the mapping class group action on the relative character variety.

events.summary: PURCHASE TICKETS Ed Dupas (du-PAW) is an Americana artist with a knack for crafting songs that stick with you—songs that balance grit and vulnerability while cutting to the heart of things. Josh Rose is a Michigan singer-songwriter whose carefully crafted songs blend Americana, folk, and roots influences. Raised in Michigan's northern woodlands and honing his voice across the Midwest, Josh has spent more than two decades touring, teaching, and building a body of work defined by thoughtful lyrics and timeless storytelling. A meticulous songwriter, he believes every word matters and strives to create songs that stay with listeners long after the final note. His four studio albums reflect a career devoted to authentic songwriting and enduring craftsmanship. Michael Crittenden is the founding member and chief songwriter of the acclaimed Michigan band Troll for Trout. His songs have been featured on radio stations across the U.S., MTV, ABC, and PaxTV. An ASCAP Songwriters Award winner and recipient of multiple Billboard and WYCE Jammie Awards, he has also taught at Lamb's Retreat for Songwriters and the Mackinac Island Songwriters Workshop.
